summary: Defines an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option that tells transit routers to look more closely at a packet instead of just forwarding it. It is used by protocols that need routers along the path to inspect certain messages. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: The IPv6 Router Alert option tells transit routers that a datagram may need special processing. Its value identifies the kind of message, while unmarked datagrams can be forwarded without this extra examination.

subtitle: An IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option that signals routers to inspect selected datagrams.

tldr.problem: Routers may need to inspect some control datagrams, but examining upper-layer data in every IPv6 datagram is costly.
tldr.mechanism: The Router Alert option in the IPv6 Hop-by-Hop header marks a datagram for closer examination and carries a value identifying the message type.
tldr.outcome: The option lets routers leave unmarked datagrams to normal forwarding. RFC 2711 has been updated by RFC 6398 and RFC 9805.

today: RFC 2711 is a Proposed Standard published in October 1999. It has been updated by RFC 6398 and RFC 9805.

sections.title: Why Routers Need an Alert
sections.content:
Some control protocols send datagrams to a destination but need routers along the path to inspect or update them. Without a marker, routers would need to parse at least part of the upper-layer data in every datagram to find those messages.

RFC 2711 defines an option in the Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) Hop-by-Hop header. Its presence signals that a router should examine the datagram more closely; its absence says that the router need not inspect the contents for this purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: The option marks datagrams that may need attention from routers on the path. Routers can use the mark instead of checking upper-layer data in every datagram.

sections.title: The Router Alert Option Format
sections.content:
The option has a type field, a length field with value 2, and a two-octet value in network byte order. The first three type bits are zero; the remaining five bits encode Hop-by-Hop Option Type number 5. The alignment requirement is 2n+0, and only one Router Alert option is allowed in a Hop-by-Hop header.

Value 0 identifies a Multicast Listener Discovery message, value 1 identifies RSVP, and value 2 identifies an Active Networks message. Values from 3 to 65535 are reserved for future assignment.
sections.plainLanguage: The option carries a two-octet value that identifies the message type. The option type is number 5, and a header can contain only one Router Alert option.

sections.title: How Routers and Destinations Process It
sections.content:
A router that recognizes the option examines the datagram far enough to decide whether more processing is needed. The protocol that uses the option must define what that processing means. If processing requires inspecting the payload, the router is performing a host function and should interpret the data as a host.

The final destination must ignore the option to avoid evaluating it again. A node that does not recognize a value must silently ignore that value and continue processing the header. Protocols that expect routers to process datagrams not addressed to them must require the option; IPv6 datagrams containing RSVP messages must include it.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers follow the rules of the protocol that uses the option. The final destination ignores it, and an unknown value does not stop header processing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unnecessary use of the option can make routers spend time examining datagrams that do not need special handling. An attacker could also flood a router with false datagrams that include Router Alert options.

A router that supports the option may limit its use by rate or by other means. The RFC does not specify an authentication mechanism for the option.
sections.plainLanguage: Too many marked datagrams can consume router resources. A router may limit how many it processes.

sections.title: Registry for Option Values
sections.content:
IANA maintains the Router Alert value field. The RFC reserves values from 3 through 65535 for future use.

New values are assigned by IETF Consensus, as described in RFC 2434. The option's existing values identify Multicast Listener Discovery, RSVP, and Active Networks messages.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA maintains the list of assigned values. A new value requires IETF consensus.
